title: A Service Mesh in Practice: Linkerd
intro: A service mesh puts a small proxy beside every pod. The proxies encrypt and authenticate every call between services (mTLS) and measure it, without any change to the applications. The SRE category used Istio for traffic policy; Linkerd is the lighter alternative and is easier to see into. Namespace shop is meshed.

steps.prompt: Check the mesh itself is healthy: control plane, certificates, and versions.
steps.fake_output:
kubernetes-api
√ can initialize the client
linkerd-identity
√ certificate config is valid
√ trust anchors are within their validity period
‼ issuer cert is valid for at least 60 days
    issuer certificate will expire on 2026-10-14T09:00:00Z
linkerd-control-plane-proxy
√ control plane proxies are healthy

Status check results are √ (1 warning)
steps.explanation: Everything works, with one warning: the mesh's issuer certificate expires in 16 days.
steps.why: Run this first for any mesh problem. That warning is the one to act on: the mesh is its own certificate authority, and when the issuer certificate expires, every proxy fails its handshake and every call in the mesh stops at once. It has caused real, total outages. Rotate it, or better, have cert-manager manage it.

steps.prompt: See the live success rate, request rate, and latency of each Deployment in namespace shop.
steps.fake_output:
NAME        MESHED   SUCCESS      RPS   LATENCY_P50   LATENCY_P95   LATENCY_P99
cart           3/3   100.00%   41.2rps           4ms          11ms          20ms
checkout       3/3    91.40%   18.6rps          12ms         480ms        1900ms
inventory      2/2   100.00%   60.1rps           2ms           6ms           9ms
payments       2/2   100.00%   17.0rps          30ms          70ms         110ms
steps.explanation: checkout succeeds 91.4% of the time with a 1.9-second p99. Everything else is healthy.
steps.why: These are golden signals for every service, measured at the proxy, with no instrumentation in the code. That's the observability half of a mesh. Latency percentiles matter more than averages: checkout's p50 is fine while one request in a hundred takes nearly two seconds.

steps.prompt: Find which of checkout's calls are failing: watch live requests to and from the checkout Deployment in namespace shop.
steps.fake_output:
req id=4:1 proxy=out src=10.1.4.21:51022 dst=10.1.7.10:8080 tls=true :method=POST :path=/v1/reserve
rsp id=4:1 proxy=out src=10.1.4.21:51022 dst=10.1.7.10:8080 tls=true :status=503 latency=1901ms
req id=4:2 proxy=out src=10.1.4.21:51030 dst=10.1.9.14:8443 tls=true :method=POST :path=/v1/charge
rsp id=4:2 proxy=out src=10.1.4.21:51030 dst=10.1.9.14:8443 tls=true :status=200 latency=31ms
steps.explanation: checkout's outbound call to POST /v1/reserve returns 503 after 1.9 seconds; its call to /v1/charge is fine.
steps.why: tap streams real requests, like tcpdump that understands HTTP and already has the TLS keys. It shows the failing path and destination in seconds. The destination, 10.1.7.10, is an inventory pod: so one inventory endpoint is slow, even though inventory's own totals look healthy. Tapping production shows request paths and headers, so access to it should be restricted.

steps.prompt: Check which connections between Deployments in namespace shop are actually protected by mutual TLS.
steps.fake_output:
SRC        DST         SRC_NS   DST_NS   SECURED
cart       inventory   shop     shop     √
checkout   inventory   shop     shop     √
checkout   payments    shop     shop     √
legacy     payments    batch    shop     ×
steps.explanation: Three connections are mTLS. Calls from legacy in the batch namespace to payments are plain text.
steps.why: A mesh only secures traffic between meshed pods. 'legacy' has no proxy, so its calls are neither encrypted nor authenticated, and by default the mesh still accepts them, which keeps things working during a migration. The mesh being installed doesn't mean everything is encrypted; this is how you check. Once every client is meshed, an authorization policy can refuse unauthenticated callers.

steps.prompt:
A mesh adds a proxy to every pod. What's the main cost to weigh before adopting one?
  a) None: it's free
  b) Operational complexity and a new critical dependency: extra latency and memory per pod, certificates to rotate, and upgrades of the proxies everywhere
  c) Applications must be rewritten
  d) It only works with one programming language
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
per pod:        one more container, ~10-50 MB, ~1 ms per hop
per cluster:    a control plane and a certificate authority to operate and upgrade
failure modes:  expired issuer certificate, proxy/control-plane version skew, sidecar start-up ordering
steps.hint: Every call now passes through two more processes that you operate.
steps.explanation: A mesh is infrastructure you now run, on the path of every request.
steps.why: Adopt one for a reason you can name: mTLS everywhere for compliance, uniform metrics across many languages, or traffic shifting. For a handful of services, libraries and network policies may do. Newer designs (Istio ambient mode, Cilium) move the proxy out of each pod and into the node to reduce the per-pod cost.
